challenges.name: fakes-stubs-mocks-quiz
challenges.title: Would this test notice the bug?
challenges.description: Two EnrollmentService tests from the double-click incident: one built from vi.fn() mocks, one built on an in-memory fake that returns the objects it stores.

questions.explanation: False. mockResolvedValue makes create() succeed on every call, so the second enroll() never throws and the catch block never runs in this test. Delete it and both assertions still hold: first.ok is true and create was called twice. The test checks the wiring (a call happened) and an assumption written by the test author (create always succeeds), not the behaviour learners depend on (a double click returns already_enrolled). The misconception is that a test that mentions the double click covers it. With a fake that refuses a second (userId, courseId), the second enroll() reaches the catch block, and an assertion on its result fails when the block is removed.

True. The fake's findById returns the very object stored in its Map, so changing e also changes the fake's stored row and the next read sees status completed. PostgreSQL returns a new object built from the row on every read; the service changed only its own copy and never called repo.update(id, { progress: 100, status: "completed" }), so the database still holds active. The misconception is that any in-memory fake behaves like the database. A fake must return copies (a contract test can check it: change a returned object and read it back), otherwise it hides exactly this kind of missing write.

challenges.name: fake-enrollment-repository
challenges.title: An in-memory fake that keeps the repository contract
challenges.description: The EnrollmentService tests needed PostgreSQL and took nine minutes, and the vi.fn() mocks that replaced it hid a 500 on double clicks. Write FakeEnrollmentRepository, an in-memory class that implements the given EnrollmentRepository interface with the same contract as the real PostgreSQL repository, so the unchanged EnrollmentService can be tested against it. Contract: create(input) stores a copy with a new id "e1", "e2", ... from a counter that is never reused (not even after a delete) and returns a copy; a second row with the same (userId, courseId), whatever its status, is refused with throw new DuplicateEnrollmentError(userId, courseId), like the unique constraint enrollments_user_course_key. findById(id) returns a copy or null. findByUser(userId) returns copies of that user's rows ordered by enrolledAt, oldest first, rows with the same enrolledAt in creation order, or []. update(id, changes) applies status and/or progress (an empty object changes nothing) and returns a copy of the updated row, or null for an unknown id. delete(id) is idempotent: true when a row was removed, false when there was none, never an exception. A caller that changes a returned object, or the object it passed to create, must not change the stored row. The interface is synchronous here to keep the runner small (the real one returns Promises). Input (read by the runner): a JSON list of steps run against one service that uses your fake - enroll (with the instant the stub clock returns), progress, cancel, leave, dashboard, and tamper (a caller changes every object the repository returned, then reads the row again). Output: one line per step, as printed by the runner.
hints: PostgreSQL hands every caller a new object built from the row. What do you have to do at each point where a row enters or leaves your repository so that the fake behaves the same way?

Look at what the service does with each result: enroll() relies on an exception of one exact class (instanceof), dashboard() relies on the order of findByUser(), and the runner's enroll and tamper steps change the objects they receive. A Map keeps insertion order, and Array.prototype.sort is stable.

A similar fake for a different contract, a store of certificates: issue(userId, courseId) { const key = userId + "|" + courseId; if (this.certs.has(key)) throw new AlreadyIssuedError(key); const cert = { code: "C" + this.next++, userId, courseId }; this.certs.set(key, cert); return { ...cert }; } - the key enforces uniqueness, the counter never goes back, and the caller gets a copy.
